findings.title: Unbounded concurrent slice hydration can create a large response and parse-memory spike
findings.what: The worker documents that a batch can contain about 19 heavy slices totaling roughly 98 MB, then maps the entire unbounded batch into Promise.all. Slow or similarly timed responses can retain many response bodies while JSON parsing and structured cloning proceed, producing avoidable peak memory and latency contention even though parsing is off the UI thread.
findings.fix: Process the batch through a small bounded-concurrency queue (for example, two or three fetches at a time) while continuing to post each completed slice immediately.
findings.acceptance: A deterministic worker test instruments active fetches for a 19-item batch and proves the configured concurrency ceiling is never exceeded, every successful slice is posted once, failures do not stop later slices, and done is posted only after all items settle; an ingest-sized probe records lower or budget-compliant peak memory.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarial second pass re-read the cited baseline lines: the file itself states the approximately 19-slice/98 MB workload, and lines 41-67 confirm the complete caller-provided array is launched through Promise.all with no semaphore, chunking, or batch-size limit. The concern is therefore current and directly reproducible rather than inferred from documentation alone.
